title: Final testing and honest claims
goals: Freeze the full evaluation procedure before testing
Report a held-out result with counts and limitations
Recognize when test feedback has become development

prerequisite.prompt: Why is validation not an untouched final test?

vocabulary: Record a fixed model and procedure before testing
A record of where data and results came from
A statement whose scope must match its evidence

blocks.text: A final test is valuable because it did not guide model choices. Freeze the model, training preprocessing, threshold, metric, missing-prediction policy and test membership. Record the version before opening test labels. A classroom result is evidence about a small chosen set, not approval for deployment.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines final testing and honest claims.

A frozen classifier is tested on 20 fictional cases: TN 12 FP 2 FN 3 TP 3, blocked positive. Accuracy is 15/20=75 percent, precision 3/5=60 percent and recall 3/6=50 percent. Its previously fitted always-clear baseline gets 14/20=70 percent. The candidate improves accuracy here but misses half the blocked cases.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Final testing and honest claims at a glance
blocks.caption: The test comparison must use the same cases and consistent rules. Report the denominator, reference-label process and sampling limitations. If the software fails on one case, report that failure; do not silently drop the case and keep the original headline denominator.

blocks.label: Why does 75 percent versus 70 percent not settle deployment? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: After seeing three missed blocked cases, the team changes its threshold. The old test has now informed development. Preserve the first result and label later scores as post-test development. A new independent test is needed for a new untouched-test claim; repeatedly splitting the same inspected rows does not erase what was learned.

A report can honestly say 15 of 20 correct on this fictional held-out set. It cannot say the model is 75 percent reliable for every child, school or future input. Do not fabricate more examples to make a result sound decisive.

blocks.label: One planned case returns no prediction. What must the report retain?

workbook.title: Calculate a final report
workbook.prompt: Calculate the worked accuracy, precision and recall with denominators.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Accuracy 15/20, precision 3/5, recall 3/6. Report TN 12 FP 2 FN 3 TP 3 and blocked positive.

workbook.title: Compare a baseline
workbook.prompt: Why does 75 percent versus 70 percent not settle deployment?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The difference is one correct case on 20; error consequences, limited coverage and missed blocked cases remain.

workbook.title: Handle a revision
workbook.prompt: The team changes a threshold after reading test errors. How should it label later results?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Post-test development on an inspected set, with the first frozen test retained; a fresh independent set is needed for another untouched-test claim.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: A new frozen test has TN 7 FP 1 FN 2 TP 2. Calculate accuracy, precision and recall and state a bounded claim.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Accuracy 9/12=75 percent; precision 2/3 about 66.7 percent; recall 2/4=50 percent. These describe these 12 held-out examples only.

workbook.title: Report a failure
workbook.prompt: One planned case returns no prediction. What must the report retain?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Retain the planned denominator and report the failed case and predefined scoring policy; disclose any metric denominator change.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. This week focuses on final testing and honest claims. Model the worked example first, collect the new W 4 case independently before feedback, and use the fresh retry to check transfer. Award credit for traceable reasoning and bounded claims, including justified uncertainty.
materials: Paper, pencils and a calculator for fractions
The fictional examples and a blank evidence table
Saved classroom project records for critique; no personal student dataset required
sessions: Use the prerequisite question: Why is validation not an untouched final test? Check the explanation before proceeding.
Read the opening and model the worked evidence. Ask students to identify freeze in context.
Complete W 1 and W 2 with support: calculate a final report; compare a baseline. Require the evidence, not only the final response.
Read the visual row by row. Collect the guided explanation and compare reasoning in pairs. Connect each conclusion to the stated evidence.
Retrieve the distinction between freeze and held out. Invite a counterexample to an overconfident claim.
Discuss the application and complete W 3: The team changes a threshold after reading test errors. How should it label later results?

Collect W4 independently before giving hints. Assess these outcomes: Freeze the full evaluation procedure before testing; Report a held-out result with counts and limitations. Record any support used.
Use W 5 and the exit response to assess limits. Give targeted feedback, then the fresh retry. Save evidence of independent understanding.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided response: The difference is one correct case on 20; error consequences, limited coverage and missed blocked cases remain. Exit response: Retain the planned denominator and report the failed case and predefined scoring policy; disclose any metric denominator change.
misconceptions: Ask for the relevant counts, units, procedure or saved record. For this week: Accuracy 15/20, precision 3/5, recall 3/6. Report TN 12 FP 2 FN 3 TP 3 and blocked positive.
A stronger claim makes a stronger project
Retain the planned denominator and report the failed case and predefined scoring policy; disclose any metric denominator change.
The new case can be copied from the example

The independent task changes the evidence. Require a fresh explanation: Accuracy 9/12=75 percent; precision 2/3 about 66.7 percent; recall 2/4=50 percent. These describe these 12 held-out examples only.
teacher.assessment: For independent W 4, require: Accuracy 9/12=75 percent; precision 2/3 about 66.7 percent; recall 2/4=50 percent. These describe these 12 held-out examples only. Fresh retry TN 8 FP 2 FN 1 TP 1: accuracy 9/12=75 percent, precision 1/3, recall 1/2. Require counts and a scope-limited statement. Mark each criterion as independent, supported or not yet demonstrated. Reassess the reasoning after feedback; do not replace the first attempt silently.
teacher.support: Provide a blank evidence table and allow a verbal explanation before writing. Highlight the given conditions without supplying the W 4 conclusion. Use freeze and held out in full sentences. Extension: alter one condition in the worked example and explain which conclusion changes and which remains supported.
teacher.next: Next week: Overfitting and model capacity. Carry forward the saved evidence and the distinction between development choices and justified claims.
